standard.title: Factors shaping identities
standard.description: analyse factors that shape identities and evaluate how individuals influence the identities of others
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can examine how power, coercion and gender stereotypes influence roles and relationships (AC9HP8P03). They have not yet analysed the broader range of societal, cultural, and community factors that shape identity, nor evaluated how individuals actively influence each other's identities.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse multiple factors that shape identities — including societal norms, cultural practices, and community belonging — and evaluate how individuals influence the identities of others.

nodes.label: Societal and cultural factors on identity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how societal norms, stereotypes and cultural practices shape how individuals see themselves
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two societal or cultural factors that influence identity and explain how each shapes self-perception in a specific context
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how societal norms, stereotypes and cultural expectations influence how young people view themselves across multiple contexts (e.g. school, sport, online); evaluate which factors are most influential and why
wider: Analyse how personal totems in First Nations Australian cultures contribute to individual identity, comparing this with how identity markers function in other cultural traditions

Investigate how cultural beliefs and practices surrounding transitions to adulthood differ across cultures, including cultures of Asia, and what this reveals about how identity is constructed differently across communities
Examine how societal norms and stereotypes specifically influence perceptions of movement competence, and how this shapes participation and identity in physical activity contexts
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot analyse how external factors shape identity cannot meaningfully evaluate how individuals influence each other's identities in Node 2 — that evaluative move requires a working understanding of which forces are already at play before individual influence is layered on top.

response_modes.reason: Identity is shaped differently across contexts — what norms operate in sport differ from those online or within family. Students need multiple distinct contexts to develop the analytical skill rather than a single worked example. First Nations and Asian cultural contexts are not optional extras; they are substantive different frameworks for understanding how identity is constructed.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of cultural frameworks here — First Nations totems, Asian transition practices, movement competence norms — each adds a genuinely distinct lens on identity construction. Students who engage the wider tier develop a comparative analytical capability rather than analysing identity only through a single dominant cultural lens.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two distinct factors (e.g. societal norms, cultural practices, stereotypes) that shape identity
Explains how each factor operates in a specific context with reference to evidence or examples
Does not conflate identity with personality — recognises identity as socially and culturally shaped

nodes.label: Individuals influencing others' identities
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate how individuals — including family, friends and community — actively influence the identities of others
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one way in which family, friends or community influence another person's identity; evaluate whether that influence is positive, limiting, or both
nodes.typical_width: Analyse the role of family, friends and community in supporting an individual's identity; evaluate strategies that could enhance their own and others' wellbeing by strengthening positive identity influences
wider: Investigate how changing social standing within First Nations Australian communities alters the roles individuals play in shaping community identity — and how this differs from Western individualist models of influence

Propose and evaluate specific strategies for how a peer, family member or community figure could actively support the positive identity development of a young person navigating competing societal expectations

Examine how movement and physical activity contexts can be deliberately structured to influence participants' identity — e.g. how a coach or team culture shapes whether someone sees themselves as an athlete

response_modes.reason: Students often describe influence without evaluating it — naming that parents influence identity without assessing whether that influence is enabling or constraining. Scaffolding the evaluative move explicitly (what is the influence, in what direction does it operate, what are its effects on wellbeing, what would a positive alternative look like) helps students reach the evaluative claim the descriptor requires.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations social standing direction and the physical activity coaching direction each add a meaningfully different context for evaluating influence — they are not repeating the same analytical move in a new setting but revealing how influence operates through different structural mechanisms. Students who engage these wider directions develop more transferable evaluative capability.
success_criteria: Identifies a specific individual or group (family, friend, community) and names their influence on another's identity
Evaluates whether the influence is enabling, constraining, or both, with reasoning
Proposes at least one strategy for enhancing positive identity influence
